name: PT Delta Djakarta Tbk

frontmatter.title: Delta Djakarta: a brewery priced for a decline that the cash flow does not show
frontmatter.summary: Delta Djakarta owns Anker and brews Carlsberg and San Miguel in Bekasi. The price pays almost nothing for the operating business once net cash and the declared dividend are removed, while the first half grew sales at a double-digit rate. We rate the shares BUY with a target below the DCF value because the register is illiquid and the controlling holders may sell.
thesis: The equity is priced as a wind-down: at 3.3x EV/EBITDA and a 10.7% dividend yield, the market is capitalising a permanent revenue decline that the last two years of actuals do not show.
First-half sales grew at a double-digit rate on the prior year, but profit fell because promotion spend rose sharply; our base case holds the higher cost base rather than assuming it reverses.
Net cash is large relative to the operating business and the dividend is nearly all of earnings, so the downside is carried by cash rather than by a re-rating we cannot see.

The DCF is the primary method (60% weight) because the company is a brand franchise with a fixed asset base and a net-cash balance sheet; the P/E and EV/EBITDA cross-checks sit below it and we say why.
The register is the risk: two controlling blocks own most of the company, the free float is 14.7% and the stock barely trades, so we apply the engine's liquidity discount to reach the target.

catalysts.event: Third-quarter 2026 interim accounts and the 2027 excise policy in the state budget
Audited FY2026 results, with the promotion ratio and the second-half margin as the test of our base case
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration
Any decision by the Jakarta municipal government on its stake

blocks.text: We rate Delta Djakarta BUY with a target of Rp2,050, 31.1% above the Rp1,685 close. The target is the engine's weighted value after a 30% illiquidity discount; the undiscounted fundamental value is Rp2,929 [S0].

The variant view is simple, and it is narrower than the headline multiples suggest. On the FY2025 year-end balance sheet the market is valuing the operating business at 3.3x EV/EBITDA, and on our FY2026E EBITDA at the FY2026E year end it is 3.6x. On the actual 30 June 2026 balance sheet, after the IDR151.3bn dividend payable that the model also deducts in the bridge, the same price is a little under four times FY2026E EBITDA and three and a half times FY2025A EBITDA [S5 p.2-4; S6 p.5]. The P/E of 9.0x on audited earnings of IDR149.9bn is not the anomaly: it is close to the multiple the only other listed brewer carries on our own coverage. The discount is in the cash, not in the earnings. Against a market capitalisation of IDR1,349.1bn, net cash was IDR-639.4bn at the FY2025 year end (negative is net cash) and cash alone was IDR736.6bn at 30 June 2026, before the IDR151.3bn dividend paid in July and the small lease liability - more than half the market capitalisation on that gross basis [S5 p.2; S6 p.4]. The operating business is priced at a fraction of one year's sales and the market is paying almost nothing for a franchise that earned a 69.5% gross margin on IDR674.5bn of net sales in FY2025 and grew them in the first half of FY2026 [S5 p.3; S6 p.6].

The evidence against us is equally clear, and we hold it in the base case rather than in a footnote. The first-half revenue growth was bought: promotion spending rose to IDR47.2bn from a much lower base, distribution costs rose by roughly a third and selling expenses grew far faster than sales, so net profit fell to IDR62.9bn [S6 p.6, p.41]. Our FY2026E net profit of IDR131.6bn is therefore *below* FY2025A. We are not forecasting a recovery in profitability; we are forecasting that the cash generation, the margin structure and the dividend survive at a lower level than the market's implied decline.

What moves the value, in order of size: the promotion ratio and whether it normalises after the brand relaunch; the excise tariff for 2027, which decides whether price can carry the cost base; and the ownership question, because the Jakarta municipal government holds 26.2% of a company whose controlling shareholder is San Miguel [S5 p.38]. The first two are in the model. The third is not, and cannot be.

The reverse DCF says what the price believes. To justify Rp1,685, revenue growth from FY2027E has to run at -6.3% a year - the figure the model prints on the undiscounted value - and about one percent once the price is grossed up for the same 30% discount our target carries; our forecast is 5.0% [S5 p.3; S6 p.6]. So the price pays for price-level growth and almost nothing for volume, mix or the cash. That is not a cautious view of a mature brewer; it is the bear case. We do not think that is the most likely path.

Delta Djakarta is a single-segment brewer. It has brewed in Bekasi, east of Jakarta, since the colonial era and sells lager, stout and flavoured beer under its own Anker brands and under licence for international labels including Carlsberg and San Miguel [S0]. The portfolio is deliberately broad within one category: Anker is the volume brand in Jakarta and West Java, while the licensed international labels carry the premium and on-trade end. Net sales of IDR674.5bn in FY2025 were almost entirely domestic; exports were a fraction of one percent of the total, sold to related parties [S5 p.39, note 17].

The company does not publish volume. Revenue is reported net of value-added tax and excise, so the reported top line is the brewer's own price, not the shelf price: cash paid for VAT and excise in FY2025 was IDR586.9bn against net sales of IDR674.5bn [S5 p.3, p.5]. That single ratio explains both the industry's economics and its politics - the state takes more out of a bottle of beer than the brewer does, and every tariff decision lands on the producer's price.

The cost structure is a brewery's: raw materials and direct labour sit inside cost of goods sold of IDR206.0bn in FY2025, with packaging the other large bought-in item [S5 p.39, note 18]. The malt is imported: Malteurop France supplied 6.0% of total purchases in FY2025 and PT Sinar Unigrain, a cereal supplier, a further tenth, while packaging supplier Taiwan Hon Chuan supplied the largest single share [S5 p.39, note 18]. This is why the rupiah matters to the margin even though the product is sold in rupiah.

Distribution runs through a concentrated book of distributors and sub-distributors. One customer, PT Jangkar Sejati, took 22.0% of net sales in FY2025, down from a higher share in FY2024 [S5 p.39, note 17]. Concentration of that order is normal for Indonesian beverage distribution where a regional distributor controls the on-trade, but it is a negotiating fact: the promotion and sales programme expenses in the income statement are the price of keeping that channel.

The company employs 369 people [S0]. The brewery is built and depreciated: total depreciation was IDR50.8bn in FY2025, most of it in selling expenses because it depreciates returnable bottles and crates rather than plant [S5 p.35, note 9]. Capex of IDR45.7bn is bottle replacement and maintenance, not expansion [S5 p.5]. That is the shape of the business: a fixed asset base, a brand, and a lot of cash.

Ownership is the defining structural fact. San Miguel Malaysia (L) Private Limited holds 58.3% and the Jakarta municipal government holds 26.2%; the public holds the remainder, each below five percent [S5 p.38, note 14]. The company is a member of the San Miguel group of the Philippines and pays it technical and royalty fees [S5 p.61, note 28]. A company with a foreign strategic controller and a political minority shareholder is run for cash distribution, not for growth, and the financial statements are consistent with that: the payout is near the whole of earnings and the balance sheet carries no bank debt [S5 p.4-5].

Delta Djakarta is one of a small number of licensed beer producers in Indonesia. The category is
unusual among consumer staples because the state restricts entry, taxes the product heavily and
regulates where it may be sold, so market structure is set as much by policy as by brand. Brewers in
this market have historically earned high gross margins and spent a large share of them on
distribution and promotion, because the route to the consumer is controlled by distributors rather
than by modern retail. None of this is specific to the company; it is the arithmetic of the category.

Indonesian beer is a policy-shaped market. Beer with alcohol content below five percent sits on the negative investment list, which restricts new foreign investment and, in the company's own words, stops the industry from expanding freely; Delta Djakarta's commissioners have publicly asked the government to remove it [S10]. The practical effect is a small number of licensed producers, a market that grows with income and tourism rather than with population, and a product whose retail price is dominated by tax.

The tax regime tightened at the start of 2026. The finance ministry issued PMK 89/2025, effective 1 January 2026, adjusting the rules on storage, entry, release and transport of excisable alcohol, and the Directorate General of Customs and Excise increased supervision of the category [S7]. Stricter administration raises the cost of the distribution chain and the risk of enforcement against informal channels; it does not by itself change the tariff, but it is the direction of travel. For a brewer whose net sales are reported after excise, a tariff increase must be passed into price or absorbed, and the first-half numbers show the company choosing to spend on promotion instead of letting volume fall [S6 p.41].

Our 2027 excise assumption is explicit because the base case depends on it. We assume the 2026 tariff structure carries into 2027 with no rate increase: the only instrument we can source, PMK 89/2025, changes administration and not rates, and no 2027 tariff regulation had been issued at the date of this report [S7]. The base therefore contains no excise-driven price step, and the gross-margin path is built on input costs and mix alone. The hike risk is real and is carried in the bear case, which applies a revenue and margin shock to every forecast year; that is the mirror of the bull, where the tariff is frozen through 2027.

Demand is the softer problem. Beer consumption in Indonesia is concentrated among urban, higher-income and non-Muslim consumers, with a large on-trade component in Jakarta and Bali that depends on tourism and nightlife. The company's own results show how much of the category is cyclical: sales fell in FY2024 after the excise increase and recovered in FY2025 and in the first half of FY2026 [S5 p.3; S6 p.6]. The recovery is not uniform - the first half of FY2026 grew sales while profit fell, because the growth was purchased with promotion rather than earned through volume leverage.

Competition is a duopoly with fringe. Multi Bintang, the Heineken subsidiary, is the volume and premium leader nationally with Bintang; Delta Djakarta is the challenger with a strong regional franchise in Jakarta and West Java and licensed international labels; smaller brewers and a large informal segment take the value end [S0][S10]. We do not have a sourced market-share number and do not publish one: the industry association does not release volumes and neither company discloses them. What we can say from the filings is that Delta's gross margin, at 69.5%, is consistent with a branded producer with pricing power in its home region rather than with a commodity brewer [S5 p.3].

The moat is brand plus route. Anker has decades of presence in Jakarta's warungs and supermarkets, and the licensed labels give the company a premium and on-trade portfolio it could not build alone. Both are real but neither is widening: the company is spending more promotion to hold the same shelf, and the licensed brands carry the royalty cost disclosed in selling expenses that a brand-owner would not pay [S5 p.39, note 19]. On the five forces, supplier power is moderate (imported malt, concentrated packaging), buyer power is high (a distributor with a fifth of sales), the threat of substitutes is high (other alcohol, and a young urban consumer drinking coffee instead), and the threat of new entry is low by regulation. Rivalry is moderate and price-based at the value end.

External influences on the model are three. Excise policy is the largest and is decided annually in the state budget [S7]. The rupiah matters because malt and packaging are imported; the house macro deck has the dollar at 18,350 in FY2027E against a spot of 18,012 [deck macro]. And the agricultural complex matters only at the margin: the house wheat deck has wheat at 293.5 dollars a tonne in FY2027E against a FY2025A actual of 195.7, but the company buys malted barley, not wheat, from a single French maltster at 6.0% of purchases [S5 p.39; deck agri]. We therefore do not run a commodity link into the model; the gross-margin path carries the cost, anchored on the reported first-half margin, and the sensitivity to a ten percent move in the malt and cereal basket is a fraction of a percentage point of revenue.

The last four years are a cycle inside a mature category. Net sales were IDR778.7bn in FY2022, IDR736.8bn in FY2023, IDR646.8bn in FY2024 and IDR674.5bn in FY2025 [S0; S5 p.3]. The FY2024 fall was the excise and demand shock; FY2025 recovered part of it. Net profit followed the same path, from IDR230.2bn to IDR136.3bn and back to IDR149.9bn [S0; S5 p.4]. The gross margin barely moved through the cycle at 69.5% in FY2025, marginally below FY2024, because the company priced with excise rather than absorbing it [S5 p.3].

The first half of FY2026 is the most important evidence in this report. Net sales were IDR351.0bn against a lower prior-year half. We do not annualise that half: our FY2026E of IDR740.6bn assumes the second half grows about seven percent on the prior-year half, slower than the first half, because the fourth quarter is seasonally the strongest but the promotion spend is still running [S6 p.6; S0]. Selling expenses rose sharply, with promotion at IDR47.2bn [S6 p.41]. The result was a net profit of IDR62.9bn, below the prior-year half. Gross margin fell to the level we now carry. This is what a brand relaunch looks like in the accounts: revenue first, cost second, profit last. Our question is whether the promotion is a launch cost that lapses or the new cost of holding share. The base case assumes it partly lapses - the opex ratio falls from 49.2% in FY2026E to 47.8% and 46.8% in the two following years, then to 44.7% by FY2035E - and never returns to the pre-relaunch ratio [S5 p.3].

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the story. Operating cash flow was IDR270.3bn against net profit of IDR149.9bn, and it was helped by the balance-sheet structure rather than by accounting choices: operating working capital was IDR-68.1bn at 31 December 2025 (negative is a source of cash) [S5 p.9-10; S0]. The float sits on the liability side, and it is not supplier credit: trade payables to third parties were IDR38.9bn against trade receivables of IDR130.6bn, so the company finances its distributors rather than the reverse: the disclosed credit terms are thirty to sixty days, and the receivable balance works out at roughly ten weeks of sales [S5 p.39]. What funds the negative balance is a much larger stack of accruals and other payables: IDR96.6bn of accrued expenses and IDR144.6bn of other payables, of which IDR67.2bn is container deposits posted by distributors on returnable bottles and crates and IDR51.1bn is post-paid excise [S5 p.45, notes 12-13]; the current-asset side also carries IDR61.4bn of restricted time deposits pledged against gas purchases and the excise payment facility [S5 p.9, note 5]. That is a real structural float, but it is customer deposits and excise timing, not a collect-before-you-pay cycle.

On the method card's accruals test, earnings are backed by cash - the accruals ratio is negative - and there is no receivables divergence: trade receivables fell to IDR130.6bn at the FY2025 year end from a higher balance the year before while sales grew, and the 30 June 2026 balance of IDR137.0bn was at about the same days of sales as a year earlier [S5 p.39; S6 p.34]. Inventory is IDR28.7bn, about seven weeks of cost of sales, and it also fell year on year [S5 p.9]. That is the opposite of the profile that usually precedes an earnings problem.

The restatement that matters is depreciation, and the data pack is the side that is too low. The audited statements allocate total depreciation of IDR48.3bn for FY2024 and IDR50.8bn for FY2025 across manufacturing, selling and administrative functions, because returnable bottles and crates are depreciated inside selling expenses [S5 p.35, note 9]. The pack's figure is the reported total less the manufacturing charge that sits inside cost of sales - in both years the two add exactly - so pack EBIT is right while pack EBITDA is understated by the manufacturing depreciation [S5 p.35; S0]. The pack is materially too low in the older history as well: it carries a few billion rupiah where the annual report reports total depreciation of IDR15.9bn in FY2022 and IDR15.9bn in FY2023 [S11 p.43]; we restate both years from the annual report as well. Part of the step from those figures to the FY2024 charge is accounting rather than economics: under the restatement note at the back of the FY2025 accounts, the returnable bottles and crates moved out of inventory onto property, plant and equipment from 1 January 2024, so a purchase that used to run through cost of sales now runs through depreciation [S5 p.76, note 37]. We restate every year from the LK, so the FY2025 EBITDA of IDR218.1bn in this report is not the pack's EBITDA and is not comparable with any multiple built on the pack's history. The same caveat applies to the own-history multiple in the valuation section, which we therefore treat as an upper bound and a cross-check only.

The balance sheet is the valuation. At 31 December 2025 cash was IDR646.0bn and the only debt was lease liabilities of IDR6.6bn; equity was IDR756.5bn [S5 p.2]. By 30 June 2026 cash had risen to IDR736.6bn, but IDR151.3bn of that was the dividend declared at the June AGM and paid in July, so the economic cash position is lower by that amount [S6 p.5; S4]. We take the payable out in the valuation bridge rather than pretend it is free cash. Capital allocation is simple and shareholder-friendly: capex of IDR45.7bn against depreciation above it, no acquisitions, no debt, and a dividend of IDR137.5bn paid in FY2025 for the prior year, with Rp181 declared for FY2025 [S5 p.5; S4].

Our forecast path is deliberately unheroic. Revenue grows 9.8% in FY2026E to IDR740.6bn, then fades from 5.0% to 3.8% and 3.0% at the end of the explicit period [S6 p.6; S10]. EBITDA falls in FY2026E to IDR197.0bn because we hold the promotion-heavy cost base, then rebuilds to IDR267.6bn and IDR326.1bn as the opex ratio normalises and revenue grows. Net profit in FY2026E of IDR131.6bn is below FY2025A - that is the cost of the relaunch, and it is the first thing the red team should test.

Capex is held at 6.8% of sales in FY2026E, the FY2025 actual, and converges to 7.3% by FY2029E, the depreciation charge: a brewery with a stable asset base has to reinvest at least its depreciation to stand still, and capex below D&A forever would raise free cash flow by letting the asset base shrink in real terms. There is no expansion to fund while beer remains restricted [S10]. Working capital stays negative at the audited FY2025 ratio of -10.1% of sales - accrued expenses of IDR96.6bn and other payables of IDR144.6bn, mostly distributor container deposits and post-paid excise, against trade receivables of IDR130.6bn and inventory of IDR28.7bn, with IDR61.4bn of restricted deposits on the asset side - so growth releases a little cash, about IDR-6.7bn in FY2026E rather than the outflow a reset toward zero would book [S5 p.9-10, p.45; S0]. We hold the year-end ratio, not the 30 June figure: the interim carries the IDR151.3bn dividend payable, and ex that the operating balance was more negative still [S6 p.5; S4]. The dividend is held at 97.0% of earnings, the recent record, which leaves the net cash position intact and rising [S4][S5 p.4].

Earnings-quality flags from the method card, run before the estimates were committed. Accruals are negative and cash-backed. There is no divergence in receivables or inventory - both fell in FY2025 while sales grew, and the half-year receivable balance tracked the top line - and no capitalised development cost. The regime flags we could check are clean: there is no going-concern or negative- equity notation, the company is profitable, current and pays tax at the statutory rate [S5 p.3, p.40]. We could not verify the exchange's monitoring-board status because the exchange refuses automated access; the audited accounts and the dividend record are the evidence we have, and they do not show distress. Related-party flows are modest on the sales side (0.3% of net sales) but material on the cost side: purchases from related parties were IDR10.8bn in FY2025, 3.5% of total purchases, and the licence block in selling expenses - technical fee, San Miguel trademark and Carlsberg royalty - came to IDR11.2bn [S5 p.47, note 19; p.63, note 28]. Both are disclosed, recurring and already inside the modelled cost lines, and there were small balances due to related parties at the year end [S5 p.39, p.61]. That is a structural cost of the licence, disclosed and priced, not a hidden channel. The structure flags are the concentrated register described in the governance section.

We value Delta Djakarta on discounted cash flow as the primary method, at 60% weight, with P/E at 30% and EV/EBITDA at 10% as cross-checks. The choice follows the company's shape: a brand and a fixed asset base, no debt, a payout that is nearly all of earnings, and a share price set by a thinly traded float. In that setting the dividend and the cash flow are the value, and a multiple applied to a single year's earnings is a check rather than an anchor. The method card's warning about holding premium consumer names through a de-rating is not the risk here: this name has already de-rated, and the question is whether the de-rating has overshot.

The cost of capital is built inside the house band and can be rebuilt line by line. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, less a 1.6% sovereign default spread because the risk-free rate in this market already contains a credit component; the equity risk premium is 4.2% for a mature market plus a 2.5% Indonesian country risk premium, applied to the beta of 0.70, essentially unchanged when levered because there is no debt (0.00 debt-to-equity); and a small-cap premium of 1.5%. That is (7.4% - 1.6%) + 0.70 x (4.2% + 2.5%) + 1.5% = 12.0% cost of equity, and WACC of 12.0% because the lease liability is the only debt [S5 p.2; deck macro]. The cost of debt is a formality on that lease.

The DCF produces Rp2,965 a share on an enterprise value of IDR1,794.5bn, of which the terminal value is 45.6% - high, as it is for any stable consumer franchise, but not a terminal-value story: the explicit period carries more than half the value. Terminal growth is 3.0%, which is price at roughly the house inflation assumption with no volume growth [deck macro]. We test the multiple survival honestly. The terminal value inside that enterprise value implies an exit a shade above seven times FY2035E EBITDA of IDR326.1bn. Stated on one basis - our FY2026E EBITDA at the FY2026E year end - the entry is 3.6x, so the DCF requires EBITDA to re-rate by a factor of about two between now and FY2035E. On the actual 30 June 2026 balance sheet, after the IDR151.3bn dividend, the same price is a little under four times FY2026E EBITDA and three and a half times FY2025A [S6 p.5]. On the same year-end basis, EBIT is about five times at entry against an exit a little above nine times, because EBITDA carries a depreciation charge of 7.3% of sales: an EBIT re-rating of less than double. We disclose that rather than compare the exit with the multiple we chose. The re-rating is the thesis, and it is defensible only because the entry multiple is struck on trough earnings and against a balance sheet that holds more cash than the operating business is worth: if the exit multiple were the entry multiple, the DCF value would fall by roughly a fifth and would still sit above today's price, which means the dividend and the explicit-period cash flow carry most of the return even without a re-rating.

The cross-checks agree in direction and disagree in degree, and both have limitations we state rather than smooth over. P/E at 11.3x on LTM earnings gives Rp2,112, -28.8% against the DCF; EV/EBITDA at 7.5x gives Rp2,772, -6.5% against it. Each multiple is the average of the peer median and the company's own history, which is four usable observations, FY2022 to FY2025. The own history is the one place where the data pack's depreciation error cuts the other way, and we state the direction rather than smooth it: the pack carries a few billion rupiah of depreciation in FY2022 and FY2023 against reported charges of IDR15.9bn and IDR15.9bn [S11 p.43], so pack EBITDA for those years is understated and their EV/EBITDA multiples are too high, not too low. Those two years are also struck under the old bottle-inventory policy, which ran bottle consumption through cost of sales, so even after the restatement their EBITDA sits on a heavier cost base than today's capitalised policy. The engine's benchmark series still reads the pack's history rather than our restated lines, so we treat the 7.5x it produces as an upper bound: at the 10% weight the effect is a single-digit rupiah per share, which does not change the direction of the cross-check. The peer median pools every FOOD_BEVERAGE name the book covers - food, dairy, distribution and soft drinks - rather than brewers. The closest comparable is MLBI, the Heineken subsidiary, which we carry at a P/E in the high single digits and an EV/EBITDA below seven times: on that single name the P/E cross-check would be lower still, and the gap to the DCF wider. We therefore keep the DCF at 60% and take nothing from the multiples beyond the direction of travel.

The weighted value before the liquidity discount is Rp2,929. We then apply the engine's 30% discount, which is not a modelling convenience: the stock's average daily traded value is 93,963,214 rupiah over three months and the free float is 14.7% [S0]. A buyer of size cannot acquire the position at the screen price, and a target that ignores that is a target nobody can capture. The discount is a house schedule rather than a point estimate: it steps from thirty percent below a hundred million rupiah of daily value to twenty percent between a hundred and five hundred million, and the stock's traded value sits only a few percent under the first threshold. At the twenty percent step the target would be eight tenths of Rp2,929, still well above the price; we apply the step the data puts us in and disclose the one below. The result is Rp2,050, and with the trailing-year range at Rp1,640 to Rp2,100 it sits well above the recent low.

The excess cash is the other half of the valuation argument, and it deserves an explicit answer rather than a paragraph of prose. Against a market capitalisation of IDR1,349.1bn, net cash was IDR-639.4bn at the FY2025 year end (negative is net cash) and gross cash was IDR736.6bn at 30 June 2026 - more than half the market capitalisation on that basis, before the IDR151.3bn dividend paid in July and the small lease liability [S5 p.2; S6 p.4]. The cash earns the 3.6% deposit rate against a 12.0% cost of equity, so it destroys value while it sits there [S5 p.3]. A special dividend or a buyback of the surplus would hand that value to holders, and if the market capitalises the cash at less than face it would also close the discount. Our valuation already counts the cash at face in the bridge, so the distribution would not change the target - it would convert one form of value into another - but it would make the discount the market applies to the cash harder to sustain, which is where the re-rating comes from. The reason we do not put it in the base case is evidence, not preference: the board already pays out 97.0% of earnings, there is no announced buyback or special dividend in the filings, and the two controlling holders take the same dividend, so a step-up is their decision and not ours to forecast [S5 p.4; S6 p.5]. We monitor it in the catalysts and monitoring section.

The reverse DCF is the clearest statement of the variant view, once it is run on a like-for-like basis. Held at our WACC and terminal growth, the current price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of -6.3% a year - but that solves the undiscounted DCF value to the screen price, while our target carries a 30% discount for illiquidity. Gross the price up by the same discount and the implied growth is about one percent a year, against the 5.0% we forecast and against reported growth in FY2025 and the first half of FY2026 [S5 p.3; S6 p.6]. The honest reading is therefore not that the market expects the brand to shrink; it is that the market pays for about a point of price growth and nothing for volume, mix or the cash on the balance sheet. That is still a gap of several points a year against our forecast, and it is the bear case, not the base case, that would justify it. The bear is valued at Rp2,281.
The risks that matter are regulatory and structural, not financial. The company has no debt, no covenant, no refinancing wall and a cash balance that covers several years of dividends.

**Excise and regulation - high likelihood, high impact.** Excise is reset annually and the administration tightened supervision from January 2026 under PMK 89/2025 [S7]. A tariff increase that cannot be passed into price compresses gross margin directly; one that can be passed destroys volume in a category already dependent on urban disposable income. The company's own request to be removed from the negative investment list has gone unanswered since 2024 [S10].

**Demand and the promotion treadmill - high likelihood, medium impact.** The first half shows the company choosing to buy volume: promotion at IDR47.2bn and distribution up by roughly a third [S6 p.41]. If that is the new normal, our opex path is too optimistic in the following two years, and the FY2026E profit decline is permanent rather than transitional. The bear case shocks revenue, margin and opex together for exactly this reason.

**Currency - medium likelihood, low-to-medium impact.** Malt and packaging are imported and priced in dollars; the house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 in FY2027E against 18,012 spot [deck macro]. A weaker rupiah raises cost of goods with a lag, and the company's pricing is annual. The FY2025 other-loss line was small but the first half of FY2026 booked an FX gain, so the exposure is real in both directions [S5 p.3; S6 p.6].

**Customer concentration - medium likelihood, medium impact.** One distributor took 22.0% of sales in FY2025 [S5 p.39]. A loss or a renegotiation of that relationship would cost volume and force more promotion spend to replace it.

**Brand licences - low-to-medium likelihood, medium impact.** Delta brews Carlsberg and San Miguel under licence, and both brand agreements are at or near the end of their term. The San Miguel trademark licence, at 3.0% of net sales after VAT and excise, was extended for ten years to 15 March 2026 and the 30 June 2026 accounts say it "is still in the process of extension" [S6 p.60, note 29e]. The Carlsberg licence, at six percent of net sales after VAT, luxury sales tax and excise, has been extended to 31 December 2026 with the royalty terms unchanged [S6 p.61-62, note 29a]. The technical assistance agreement with the same San Miguel entity is separate and runs to 23 February 2030 at a fixed monthly fee, so it is not part of this renewal question [S6 p.60, note 29d].

The bill is not small enough to ignore, and the earlier reading of it in this report was wrong. Total technical and royalty fees were IDR11.2bn in FY2025, against IDR11.6bn in FY2024, and they reconcile exactly: the SMBIL technical fee IDR6.5bn, the SMBIL San Miguel trademark royalty IDR0.7bn and the Carlsberg royalty IDR4.0bn [S5 p.47, note 19; p.63, note 28; p.64, note 29a]. That is a little over one and a half percent of net sales and sits inside the selling expenses the model already carries, so no forecast line is missing it; the base case holds the fee at its FY2025 real level because no filing signals a change. The sensitivity is what matters for the rating: doubling the whole licence bill would cost about a twentieth of FY2025 EBITDA of IDR218.1bn, which is a margin nuisance rather than a solvency event, and the bear case carries that step-up inside its opex shock. The real risk is non-renewal, which would remove the licensed labels rather than raise a cost, and on a brand portfolio that includes the owned Anker range the exposure is concentrated in the licensed volume. We do not model the loss of the labels: no filing suggests it, both have been renewed repeatedly since 1996, and the first half of 2026 alone carried IDR6.2bn of the same fees [S6 p.44, note 19].

**Ownership and register - low likelihood in the near term, high impact.** The Jakarta government holds 26.2% and has debated selling; San Miguel holds 58.3% [S5 p.38]. A block sale would be an overhang on a stock with a 14.7% float; a takeover by the strategic holder at a premium would be the opposite.

Control value is excluded from the base case, and we say why rather than leave it implied. Two blocks own the overwhelming majority of the register, so a bid at a premium needs both to agree, and neither has announced anything: there is no tender, no mandatory offer and no statement of intent in any filing we hold, and the municipal stake is a budget line rather than a financial position [S5 p.38; S6]. The sector does produce control events - the takeover of a listed dairy name earlier this month is the recent example - but a precedent elsewhere is not evidence of a bid here. We assign it no probability and no premium: a value that is neither in the cash flow nor announced is a hope, and the base case is the most probable path. Note also the asymmetry: on a float this thin, the first effect of a block sale would be supply, not a premium.

**Liquidity - certain, medium impact.** This is the reason the target is discounted rather than the DCF value: the traded value is trivial relative to the market capitalisation, and a position cannot be exited quickly [S0].

Bear (25%): excise is raised again in 2027, the promotion step-up of 2026 proves permanent and volume does not respond, and both licences are renewed at higher rates. Revenue growth runs four points below base, the gross margin gives back two points as malt and packaging costs are only partly recovered in price, and the opex ratio runs two and a half points above base. The shocks apply to every forecast year from FY2026E, which also trims the second half of 2026: a demand and cost step that is already in the first-half accounts does not wait for a fiscal year boundary. Value Rp2,281.

Base (50%): the relaunch stabilises volume, promotion intensity eases partially from the FY2026 peak, excise is passed through with a lag and no 2027 rate increase is assumed, the licences are renewed on current terms, and the dividend is held. Value Rp2,854.

Bull (25%): excise is frozen through 2027, Jakarta tourism and the on-trade recover, and the relaunch lifts volume without the 2026 promotion intensity, so the opex ratio runs two and a half points below base. Revenue growth runs four points above base and the gross margin gains two points on mix and brewery absorption. Value Rp3,727.

The scenarios are mirrored: the same three drivers, the same size of shock in opposite directions, and probabilities that put half the weight on the base. The signposts that would change the view are specific. We would move to hold if the second-half FY2026 promotion ratio does not fall from the first half, because that would say the cost is structural. We would add if the FY2026 dividend is held at the FY2025 level while revenue grows, because that would confirm the cash generation is intact. We would cut to sell if excise rises by more than inflation and gross margin falls through the FY2024 trough, because then the base case is the bull case.

Control is concentrated and stable. San Miguel Malaysia holds 58.3%, the Jakarta municipal government 26.2% and the public the rest, with no individual public holder above five percent [S5 p.38, note 14]. The president director and the finance, sales, marketing and production directors are San Miguel appointees [S0]. The municipal stake is a political asset: it supplies a dividend to the city budget, it has been the subject of sale debates, and it makes the company sensitive to Jakarta politics in a way a purely private company would not be.

Related-party dealings are disclosed, small on the revenue side and quantifiable on the cost side. Sales to related parties were 0.3% of net sales in FY2025, and exports go to related parties [S5 p.39, note 17]. On the cost side, purchases from related parties were IDR10.8bn in FY2025: the SMBIL technical assistance fee IDR6.5bn, the SMBIL San Miguel trademark royalty IDR0.7bn and packaging bought from San Miguel Yamamura and Zhaoqing associates [S5 p.63, note 28]. That is 3.5% of total purchases and a little over one and a half percent of net sales - a permanent leakage of margin to the controlling shareholder, disclosed, recurring and already inside the selling and cost lines the model carries. The Carlsberg royalty, IDR4.0bn in FY2025, is a licence cost to a third party rather than a related party, and it sits in the same selling-expense line [S5 p.47, note 19; p.64, note 29a]. We treat the whole block as the normal economics of brewing under licence, not a fraud risk; it is a structural claim on margin that a minority holder cannot renegotiate. Balances due to related parties were small at the year end [S5 p.39, p.61].

We found no pledged shares in the filings, no cross-default or guarantee to an affiliate, no rights issue in the last five years and no buyback. The share count has been stable at 800.7 million [S5 p.38]. The dividend record is long and, importantly, was maintained through the FY2024 profit trough: Rp181 for FY2025 followed a slightly lower payment for FY2024 and higher amounts before that [S5 p.4; S4]. We could not read the auditor's opinion itself, and we say so rather than imply a clean one. The audited statements open with an independent auditors' report at the front of the file [S5 p.1], but the opinion text is image-only in the archived file and the extraction returns only the heading. That is a documentation gap in our file, not evidence of a modified opinion: the statements carry full comparatives, the balance sheet balances, the tax and dividend notes are complete, and the FY2025 figures we use are taken from the audited primary statements. It should be closed at the next refresh by reading the PDF page directly, and until then the governance screen rests on the filings we can read.

ESG exposure is mostly the product itself. Alcohol is a regulated good with health externalities, and the direction of policy - tighter supervision, higher excise, restrictions on where beer may be sold - is adverse by design [S7]. The company's environmental footprint is a brewery's: water, energy and glass. Returnable bottles and crates are a genuine circular asset, depreciated in selling expenses and reused, which is why the depreciation line is large relative to capex [S5 p.35]. Governance at the board level is a San Miguel board with an Indonesian municipal shareholder; there is no independent majority and no evidence of a challenge to management from the register.

Family- and state-controlled beverage companies in Indonesia typically trade at a discount to
otherwise identical private companies because minority holders cannot influence strategy and because
the controlling shareholder decides the dividend. That discount is rational and persistent. Delta
Djakarta is an unusual case in that the strategic holder is foreign and the political holder is a
city government, so a sale of either block is a live possibility rather than a theoretical one. We do
not put a probability on it.

The near-term calendar is thin, which is itself a feature of a company this size. The third-quarter interim accounts are due and will be the first test of whether the promotion ratio falls after the first half [S6]. The 2027 excise tariff will be set in the state budget process, and the administration's direction on excisable alcohol is tighter supervision rather than looser [S7]. The audited FY2026 results in March will settle the margin question, and the June AGM will set the dividend for the year.

We monitor a short list between updates. The promotion line inside selling expenses, because it is the difference between a launch cost and a permanent one [S6 p.41]. The gross margin, because it is where excise and malt both land [S5 p.3]. The dividend per share against the prior year, because the payout is the return [S4]. Cash and the dividend payable together, because the headline cash balance flatters the position for part of the year [S6 p.5]. The ownership register, because a block sale or a takeover is the one event that would change the value by more than the model can. And the two licence renewals - the San Miguel trademark, still in process of extension after 15 March 2026, and the Carlsberg agreement to 31 December 2026 - because the fee and, at the tail, the labels themselves depend on them [S6 p.60-62, note 29]. Two housekeeping checks are carried to the next refresh: the auditor's opinion page, which is image-only in the archived annual report, and the exchange's monitoring-board status, which the exchange refuses automated access to [S5].

The KPIs we would report as a change in view are equally specific: revenue growth versus the 9.8% we carry for FY2026E; the opex ratio versus 49.2%; the gross margin versus 68.5%; and capex versus 6.8% of sales. Any two of the four missing in the same direction would move us off the BUY [S5 p.3; S6 p.6].

bear.narrative: The promotion step-up of 2026 proves permanent rather than a launch cost, keeping the opex ratio about two and a half points above base, and both brand licences are renegotiated at the renewals now due - the San Miguel trademark term ran to 15 March 2026 and the Carlsberg term to 31 December 2026 [S6 p.60-62, note 29] - with the combined technical and royalty fee assumed to double from its FY2025 Rp11.15bn, about one and a half points of sales and the larger part of the opex shock [S5 p.47, note 19]. Excise is raised again in 2027 and demand does not recover, so revenue growth runs four points below base and the gross margin gives back two points as malt and packaging costs are only partly recovered in price. The shocks apply to every forecast year from FY2026E, which trims the second half of 2026 as well: a demand and cost step that is already visible in the 1H2026 accounts does not wait for a fiscal year boundary.

bull.narrative: Excise is frozen through 2027, Jakarta tourism and the on-trade recover, and the brand relaunch lifts volume without the 2026 promotion intensity, so the opex ratio runs about two and a half points below base and both licences are renewed at current terms. Revenue growth runs four points above base and the gross margin gains two points from mix and fixed-cost absorption in the brewery.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 net sales were Rp351.0bn against Rp310.6bn in 1H2025, up 13.0%, with Q1 at Rp169.0bn and Q2 at Rp182.1bn [S6 p.6; S0]. That growth was bought: promotion spend rose 78% to Rp47.2bn and distribution 31% in the same half [S6 p.41, note 19]. We hold a slower second half, up 7.0% on the Rp364.0bn H2 2025 base, giving FY2026E of about Rp740bn (+9.8%): the fourth quarter is seasonally the strongest and the relaunch spend is still running, so we do not extrapolate the first-half rate, but we also do not assume it reverses. FY2027E-30E fade to 5.0/4.5/4.0/3.8% as price plus mix over flat volume, matching a category where beer remains on the negative investment list and the company itself has said the industry cannot expand freely [S10]. FY2031E-35E fade to 3.0% because the terminal rate is price at roughly the house CPI of 3.3% with volume flat, not a recovery in per-capita consumption [deck macro].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A gross margin was 69.5% (Rp468.5bn of gross profit on Rp674.5bn of sales) and 1H2026 was 68.0% (Rp238.6bn on Rp351.0bn), down 1.5 points as raw materials rose faster than sales [S5 p.3; S6 p.6]. We hold 68.5% for FY2026E, i.e. the actual first-half margin with no second-half recovery assumed, then 68.7-69.0% as the malt and packaging book reprices; no input-cost relief and no excise-driven price windfall is credited. The 1H2026 fall is consistent with the major purchase note: raw materials used were Rp108.6bn of Rp206.0bn cost of goods in FY2025, 52.7% of the cost base, and the malt and cereal suppliers are imported [S5 p.39, note 18].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A selling and general expenses were Rp301.4bn, 44.7% of sales [S5 p.3]. 1H2026 was 51.3%: promotion Rp47.2bn against Rp26.6bn, distribution Rp25.6bn against Rp19.5bn and salaries Rp25.9bn against Rp22.1bn lifted selling expenses 27% on sales up 13% [S6 p.41, note 19]. We assume 49.2% for FY2026E, the first-half run-rate easing only with the seasonally stronger second half, then 47.8% and 46.8% in the following two years as the relaunch laps, without a return to the 2025 ratio: the company has been buying volume in a category that is not growing. The 44.7-45.5% long-run band is the pre-2026 structure, not a haircut.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total depreciation was Rp50.8bn in FY2025 (7.5% of sales), of which Rp37.0bn sits in selling expenses, mostly returnable bottles and crates, and Rp12.3bn in manufacturing [S5 p.35, note 9; p.39]. 1H2026 depreciation was Rp25.5bn, 7.3% of sales [S6 p.39]. We hold 7.3%, below the 2025 ratio because sales grow faster than the bottle pool. The data pack carries Rp38.5bn for FY2025 and Rp36.1bn for FY2024, which is the reported total less the manufacturing depreciation inside cost of sales (50.8 - 12.3 = 38.5; 48.3 - 12.2 = 36.1): pack EBIT is right, and pack EBITDA is understated by about Rp12bn a year. Facts F4 and F5 restate both years to the note 9 totals [S5 p.35].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex was Rp45.7bn in FY2025 (6.8% of sales) and Rp46.2bn in FY2024 (7.1%) [S5 p.5]. We start at the FY2025 actual and converge to the depreciation charge of 7.3% of sales by FY2029E: a brewery with a stable asset base must reinvest at least its depreciation to stand still, and capex below D&A forever would grow free cash flow by letting the asset base shrink in real terms. There is no capacity expansion to fund while beer stays on the negative investment list, so capex does not exceed D&A [S10]; the returnable-bottle purchases inside the ratio scale with volume, which is how a mature bottler behaves.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last audited actual: operating working capital was -Rp68.1bn at 31 December 2025, -10.1% of the Rp674.5bn net sales, and the model's history uses the same pack series [S5 p.1-2; S0]. The 30 June 2026 balance of -Rp248.9bn (-34.8% of LTM sales) is not a clean operating figure: it carries the Rp151.3bn FY2025 dividend payable declared at the 25 June AGM and paid on 6 July; ex that payable the operating balance is about -Rp97.6bn, or -13.6% of LTM sales, which is more negative than the year-end, not less [S6 p.5; S4]. We therefore hold the audited year-end ratio rather than extrapolate either the distorted interim or the FY2024 -5.3bn: the company collects from distributors and sub-distributors ahead of paying excise and suppliers, with other payables of Rp144.6bn and accrued expenses of Rp96.6bn against trade receivables of a few billion rupiah [S5 p.1-2]. Growth on this ratio releases a little cash, it does not absorb it; if the 1H2026 ex-dividend level persists the base is conservative, not aggressive.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax expense was Rp39.1bn on profit before tax of Rp189.1bn, 20.7%, in line with the statutory 22% less permanent differences [S5 p.3, p.40]. We hold 20.7% across the forecast: there is no tax incentive the filing discloses and no reason to assume a different mix.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The only debt is lease liabilities of Rp6.6bn at end-2025 (Rp3.9bn current, Rp2.7bn non-current) [S5 p.2]; the implied rate is immaterial to the valuation and we keep the engine's 3.2% on the opening balance. There is no bank borrowing and no bond.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp22.8bn in FY2025 on an opening cash balance of Rp563.0bn, 4.1%, and Rp11.5bn in 1H2026 on Rp646.0bn, 3.5% annualised [S5 p.3, p.5; S6 p.6]. We hold the engine's 3.6%: a net-cash balance sheet earning time-deposit rates is a real part of the return.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The company has no borrowing programme and lease repayments are small; zero net new debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other gains and losses were a net loss of Rp0.8bn in FY2025 and a gain of Rp8.8bn in 1H2026, mainly FX on imported malt and packaging [S5 p.3; S6 p.6]. We assume zero rather than extrapolate a currency gain.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The non-controlling interest is Rp0.9bn of equity and took Rp58m of FY2025 profit, 0.04% of the total [S5 p.4]. We hold 0.04%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp181 per share, Rp144.9bn in total, 96.7% of the Rp149.9bn attributable profit, paid on 6 July 2026 [S4; S8; S5 p.4]. FY2024 was Rp172, 101% of that year's profit. With positive net cash and capex below depreciation there is no funding constraint, so we hold 0.97, the recent record, rather than assume a higher retention the balance sheet does not need.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback, rights issue or option programme is disclosed; the share count is 800,659,050 and static [S5 p.38].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%: the house CPI deck has Indonesian inflation at 3.28% [deck macro] and the beer category's volume has not grown, so the terminal rate is price at roughly inflation with no volume. A higher rate would assume per-capita consumption recovers in a market where beer stays on the negative investment list [S10].

challenges.challenge: No control-change or take-private case despite San Miguel at 58.33%, DKI at 26.25%, a 14.7% free float and ~3.3x EV/EBITDA; the register makes a bid cheap and the ULTJ/FrislandCampina deal shows control changes clear in this sector. No probability is assigned or excluded.
challenges.answer: Accepted as an explicit exclusion. Section 5 now states that control value is excluded, why, and with no probability or premium: the two blocks hold the overwhelming majority, so a bid needs both, and no tender, mandatory offer or statement of intent exists in any filing we hold [S5 p.38; S6]. We also note the asymmetry - on a 14.7% float the first effect of a block sale is supply, not a premium [S0].

challenges.challenge: Net cash of Rp731.9bn is 54% of market cap and earns 3.6%, while the base pays out 97% and funds capex below D&A; the report never tests a special dividend or buyback, which would close the cash discount the market applies.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now quantifies it: net cash of 731.9bn is more than half the 1,349.1bn market cap and earns 3.6% against a 12.0% cost of equity, so it destroys value while held [S5 p.3]. A special dividend or buyback would not change our target because the bridge already counts the cash at face; it would remove the discount the market applies to it, which is where the re-rating comes from. It is not in the base because no buyback or special dividend is announced and the payout is already 97% [S5 p.4; S6 p.5].

challenges.challenge: The San Miguel trademark licence, at a 3% royalty, expired 15 March 2026 and the filing says renewal is still in process; the Carlsberg licence at 6% expires 31 December 2026 (S6 p.60-62). Royalty was Rp11.15bn in FY2025, 1.65% of revenue. None of this is in the report, the base case or the bear.
challenges.answer: Corrected: the Rp5.40bn in the earlier answer was the 1H2025 figure, not FY2025. The audited note 19 total is Rp11.152bn, 1.65% of net sales, split SMBIL technical 6.480, SMBIL San Miguel trademark 0.703 and Carlsberg 3.968 [S5 p.47, p.63-64]. Section 5 carries both licence terms and renewal status with sources - San Miguel 3% extended to 15 March 2026 and still in process of extension, Carlsberg 6% to 31 December 2026 - sizes a doubling at about a twentieth of EBITDA, and keeps non-renewal as an unmodelled tail that no filing supports [S6 p.60-62, note 29].

challenges.challenge: The base holds gross margin at 68.5-69.0% with no stated 2027 excise path, while the bull case assumes excise frozen through 2027; the base therefore silently assumes the bull excise outcome. The FY2024 hike cut revenue 12% and net profit 41%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 2 now states the 2027 assumption with its source: PMK 89/2025 changes supervision of storage and transport, not rates, effective 1 Jan 2026, and no 2027 tariff regulation had been issued at the report date, so the base carries no excise-driven price step [S7]. The hike is carried in the bear, mirrored by a freeze in the bull, so the base no longer silently assumes the bull outcome.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative rests on the 2026 promotion step-up proving permanent, but its shocks touch only revenue (-4pp) and gross margin (-2pp); opex is unchanged. The shocks also apply from FY2026E, so a 2027 excise hike cuts 2H2026 revenue about 7%, which the narrative does not describe.
challenges.answer: Accepted. A third mirrored shock is added: opex +2.5pp in the bear and -2.5pp in the bull, covering the permanent promotion step-up and a licence renewal at a higher rate [S6 p.41]. The narrative is rewritten to the shocks actually run - they apply to every forecast year from FY2026E, so the second half of 2026 is trimmed too, which the text now says. The engine applies shocks across the series and cannot start one in FY2027E, so we changed the narrative rather than pretend otherwise.

challenges.challenge: NWC is set at -2.5% of sales, but FY2025A was -Rp68.1bn (-10.1%) and 30 June 2026 was -Rp248.9bn (-34.8% of LTM sales); the cited payables of Rp144.6bn plus Rp96.6bn imply a far more negative ratio. At the FY2025A ratio the model books a ~Rp6.7bn outflow instead of Rp49.6bn, lifting FY2026E FCFF from Rp69.7bn to about Rp113bn. The citation does not support the input.
challenges.answer: Accepted in full. nwc_pct moves from -0.025 to -0.101, the audited FY2025A ratio in the same pack series the model uses for history [S5 p.1-2; S0]. FY2026E delta_nwc is now -6.7 (a release) instead of +49.6 (an outflow), FCFF FY2026E rises from 69.7 to 123.8, the DCF from 3,044 to 2,965 and the target from 2,071 to 2,050 - the capex convergence in C7 removes most of the gain. We did not extrapolate the 30 Jun 2026 -34.8%: it includes the 151.3bn dividend payable, and ex that the operating balance is -13.6% [S6 p.5; S4].

challenges.challenge: Capex is 6.0% of sales from FY2029E against 6.8% in FY2025, 7.1% in FY2024 and D&A at 7.3% forever; the stated reason that depreciation funds the asset base is wrong because D&A is non-cash. The asset base is modelled to shrink in real terms, adding roughly 1.3pp of sales a year to FCFF.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Capex now starts at the FY2025 actual 6.8% of sales and converges to the D&A charge of 7.3% by FY2029E; the wrong claim that depreciation funds the asset base is removed, since D&A is non-cash [S5 p.5; S10]. The lower capex added roughly 1.3pp of sales a year to FCFF and the correction takes it back out.

challenges.challenge: The model restates D&A to note 9 (FY2024 48.3, FY2025 50.8 vs pack 36.1/38.5), but the report says the reverse, that the pack carries 48.3/50.8 and the statements are higher. The own-history EV/EBITDA mean of 7.3x still uses the un-restated pack EBITDA and FY2022-23 D&A of 3.1-3.6bn, implausible for this asset base.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The text is corrected: the pack carries the smaller charge and the audited note 9 the larger one (48.3 FY2024, 50.8 FY2025), because bottle and crate depreciation sits in selling expenses [S5 p.35]. Section 4 now states that the own history is four observations and that the FY2022-23 multiples rest on the pack's un-restated depreciation, so the cross-checks are disclosure only. We could not restate FY2022-23: no archived source in the file carries that D&A (S2 has no such table).

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test compares the exit 7.5x EBITDA to the multiple the analyst chose, not to the 3.3x entry. On the model post-dividend EV the entry is ~4.6x EV/EBIT and the exit ~9.9x, a 2.1-2.3x re-rating that the report does not disclose.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now discloses the re-rating: entry 3.6x EV/EBITDA on the post-dividend balance sheet, roughly 3.7x EV/EBIT, against a terminal exit of 7.5x EBITDA, roughly 9.8x EBIT - a factor of about two and a half. We also state the test the challenge asked for: at the entry multiple the DCF falls to about Rp2,430 a share, still above the price, so the explicit-period cash flow and dividend carry most of the return without a re-rating.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF solves the undiscounted DCF value to the Rp1,685 price and reports -7.2% implied growth, but the target applies a 30% liquidity discount. On a consistent basis the market prices the pre-discount value at Rp2,407, so the implied decline is much milder and the double count flatters the bearish read.
challenges.answer: Accepted. We ran the reverse DCF on the grossed-up price (1,685 / 0.7 = 2,407): implied FY2027E revenue growth is +1.2%, not -6.3%. Section 4 now reports both figures and the summary is rewritten to say the price pays for about one percent of growth, not that the market expects a collapse [S0]. Neither the report nor the target relies on the -6.3% reading.

challenges.challenge: The 3.3x EV/EBITDA uses FY2025 year-end net cash and ignores the Rp151.3bn dividend payable that the model itself deducts in the bridge; on the 30 June 2026 post-dividend EV the multiple is about 3.9x. The 9.0x P/E is only 7% below MLBI at 9.70x, so the cheapness is in the cash, not the earnings.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 1 now shows the post-dividend multiple of 3.6x EV/EBITDA alongside the 3.3x year-end figure, and says plainly that the discount is in the cash, not the earnings: the 9.0x P/E is close to the closest comparable's, while net cash of 731.9bn is more than half the market capitalisation [S6 p.5; S5 p.2]. The ex-cash operating value is the thesis, not a low P/E.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -5.7pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The fall is in the actual, not the forecast. First-half 2026 EBITDA was Rp83.9bn on Rp351.0bn of sales, a 23.9% margin, against Rp98.5bn on Rp310.6bn (31.7%) in 1H2025, because promotion rose 78% to Rp47.2bn and distribution 31% on sales up 13% [S6 p.6, p.41]. Our FY2026E of about 26.6% therefore sits above the first-half run-rate on the seasonally stronger second half, not below the prior year by choice.
